newsitem.title: FINLAND: NO PRESSURE ON STABLE MARKKA IN ERM-LINK - LIPPONEN.
newsitem.headline: NO PRESSURE ON STABLE MARKKA IN ERM-LINK - LIPPONEN.

text.p: Finland's decision to link the markka to Europe's Exchange Rate Mechanism ERM is unlikely to lead to any pressure on its external value, Prime Minister Paavo Lipponen said at the weekend.
"The markka has been a stable currency for a couple of years," Lipponen told a news conference on Saturday evening.
"Because (it) has been stable for a relatively long time it can be assumed that the ERM-link will not cause any special pressures on the exchange rate," he said.
"The Finnish economy is stable. We will continue with the economic policy we have embraced," Lipponen said.
"And since there is confidence in the Finnish economy there is every reason to expect that no particular pressures will arise," he said.
The ERM's wide fluctuation limits, plus-minus 15 percent, would provide shelter against "unwarranted speculation," the government said in a statement.
The markka-ERM link had been prepared since last spring and had included contacts with central banks and governments of other European Union countries, Lipponen said.
"From these contacts we have been able to draw the conclusion that there is a strong feeling of confidence in the stability of the Finnish economy," Lipponen said.

The main reason to end the 49-month floating of the Finnish currency by pegging it to ERM was "to make sure in every way that Finland will fulfil the conditions for Europe's Economic and Monetary Union at the stage when decisions about joining the third phase are made," Lipponen said.
The third stage of the single currency is scheduled to start in January 1999.

"Through participation in the Exchange Rate Mechanism, the Finnish government wants to guarantee that Finland will fulfil all the convergence criteria related to the third state of Economic and Monetary Union," the government said in a statement.
Lipponen noted that the ERM link was necessary to give the national parliament a real choice when deciding, probably in autumn 1997, whether to join the single currency.
"We really made sure ... that when parliament ultimately decides on the issue it will also have the alternative that we can join among the first," Lipponen said.

Asked if Finland had received assurances from other EU countries that it would qualify even though the markka would have been in ERM for less than two years prior to the summit of EU heads of state and government in spring 1998, Lipponen said:

"From the view reached by the government, based on conversations mainly with political leaders in EU countries, one can draw the conclusion that (the duration of) this (ERM) participation will be sufficient."
